analysis.one_liner: Requires drug makers to share FDA drug data with the patent office, so weak patents can be challenged.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2023 with bipartisan sponsorship but never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Drug companies sometimes describe their data differently to two government agencies: they tell the Food and Drug Administration one thing to win drug approval, then tell the patent office another thing to win broader, longer-lasting patents. This bill would require drug companies to certify that the information they give both agencies is consistent, hand over any FDA submissions relevant to a patent's validity to the patent office, and allow a company accused of patent infringement to escape liability if the patent holder hid required information. The aim is to make it harder to keep cheaper generic and biosimilar competitors off the market with patents built on inconsistent filings.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who buy prescription drugs, because more effective challenges to weak drug patents should speed the arrival of lower-priced generic and biosimilar competition; and generic and biosimilar manufacturers, who gain a defense against patent suits when a brand-name company failed to disclose required information.

how_it_helps.text: Requires drug application sponsors and holders of approved applications to certify to the FDA that their information is complete and consistent with what they told the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, and to submit to the patent office any FDA material relevant to a patent's validity. [S2]

Adds a legal defense for a person accused of infringing a drug patent if the patent owner negligently or intentionally failed to disclose information the bill requires, which could invalidate patents built on hidden or inconsistent information. [S2]

Makes compliance a condition of FDA approval: the FDA may reject a drug application if the sponsor failed to comply with the disclosure certification, and noncompliance becomes a prohibited act subject to FDA enforcement. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name and biologic drug manufacturers, who would face new certification and disclosure duties with every application and patent, could see patents narrowed or invalidated, and would lose a common tool for delaying generic and biosimilar competition.

drawbacks.text: The bill's enforcement tool reaches negligent failures to disclose, not just intentional ones, so a patent could be undermined by an honest mistake in a large filing, weakening patent incentives for legitimate inventions. [S2]

Companies would bear new compliance costs and might file more cautiously with the FDA to avoid creating information that undercuts their patents, adding administrative burden to the drug approval process. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The mechanism is narrow and targeted: it does not change patent law directly, it just closes the gap between what drug companies tell the FDA and what they tell the patent office. The main cost falls on drug makers in extra compliance work and some risk to patents over negligent mistakes. For patients, the benefit depends on how much patent-thicket strategies actually delay generics, which research suggests is substantial for many drugs; the bill addresses one known contributor but not the whole problem.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Maggie Hassan introduced the bill on September 13, 2023, for herself and Sen. Mike Braun, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions. [S4]
That referral was the last action ever recorded; the bill received no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no further amendments before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025. [S4]
Sen. Braun was the bill's only cosponsor besides its sponsor. [S3]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers are better off: the patents and filing practices the bill targeted remain untouched, and no competing version advanced in the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat sponsored the bill and a Republican was its only cosponsor; no opposition ever appeared on the record because the committee never acted, so the partisan shape beyond the two sponsors is unknown.

industries.note: The bill targets a known strategy: getting broad drug patents using characterizations of data that differ from what the company told the FDA, then using those patents to block cheaper generics and biosimilars. It would expose those patents to challenge and require disclosure of FDA communications to the patent office.
A non-disclosure defense against patent infringement would make it easier to launch lower-priced copies and survive patent suits built on withheld information.
